source_text: Ζητήσας δὲ μεμελημένος, καὶ σοφῶς κατανοήσας τὴν περὶ γῆν φύσιν ἅπασαν, ποικιλωτάτην ἔγνων, ὡς ἀνθρώπῳ δέδοται πονεῖν ἐπὶ γῆς, ἄλλοτε ἀλλοίᾳ καμάτου προφάσει ἐγκαλινδουμένῳ εἰς τὸ μηδέν. Πνεύματος δὲ ἀλλοκότου καὶ μυσαροῦ τὰ κάτω ἅπαντα πλήθει, ὥστε μὴ εἶναι αὐτὰ ἀνακτήσασθαι, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἀναθυμηθῆναι τὸ παράπαν ὅση τὰ κατὰ ἀνθρώπους πράγματα κατείληφεν ἀτοπία. Λογισάμενος γάρ ποτε ἐγὼ κατ᾽ ἐμαυτόν, καὶ οἰηθεὶς ὡς ἁπάντων εἴην τότε τῶν πρὸ ἐμαυτοῦ γεγονότων ἐνταυθοῖ σοφώτερος· ἔγνων παραβολάς τε συνεῖναι καὶ πραγμάτων φύσεις. ᾨήθην δὲ τηνάλλως ἐπὶ τούτῳ φέρεσθαι, καὶ σοφίᾳ μὲν γνῶσιν ἕπεσθαι, γνώσει δὲ πόνους ἐπακολουθεῖν.
thought_title: Searching out wisdom brings only toil
orientation: Solomon searches out the nature of things and finds that wisdom and knowledge lead only to toil.
pass_a_gloss: Having sought with diligence and having wisely observed the entire nature of things about the earth, I knew it as most manifold: namely that to a human being it has been given to labor upon the earth, he being rolled about at one time on one pretext of weariness and at another time on another, into nothing. All things below are filled with an alien and abominable spirit, with the result that it is not possible to recover or restore them, but not even at all to call to mind or reckon up how great an absurdity has seized the affairs among human beings. For having once reasoned by myself, and having supposed that I was then wiser than all who had come to be here before me, I determined to understand both parables and the natures of things. And I supposed that I was borne along idly, to no purpose, in this; and that knowledge follows upon wisdom, and toils follow after knowledge.

pass_b_english: I searched with care and considered wisely the whole nature of things on the earth, and I found it most varied: it has been given to human beings to toil on the earth, wallowing now on one occasion of toil and now on another, and all for nothing (Ecclesiastes 1:13). Everything here below is full of a strange and foul spirit (Ecclesiastes 1:14), so that these things cannot be set right, nor can anyone even begin to reckon how much disorder has taken hold of human affairs (Ecclesiastes 1:15).

For once I reasoned with myself, and supposed that I was then wiser than all who had lived here before me (Ecclesiastes 1:16), and I set my mind on understanding parables and the natures of things. But I came to think that in this I was carried along to no purpose (Ecclesiastes 1:17), and that knowledge follows wisdom, and toil follows knowledge (Ecclesiastes 1:18).
notes: The whole section paraphrases Ecclesiastes 1:13-18; citations are placed beside the clauses that render each verse. 'Spirit' (πνεῦμα) in 'a strange and foul spirit' renders Gregory's reading of the LXX 'choice of spirit' (προαίρεσις πνεύματος, Ecclesiastes 1:14) as an evil spirit; kept lower case. ἔγνων with the infinitive (συνεῖναι) is taken as 'I set my mind on / determined to' (compare Ecclesiastes 1:17 LXX 'I gave my heart to know'), not 'I learned to'. ἀναθυμηθῆναι is rendered 'reckon' (call to mind, count up), matching Ecclesiastes 1:15 'what is lacking cannot be numbered'. No doubtful readings in the copy-text.
